Grande femme au regard curieux, Jalia* s: A tall woman with a curious gaze, Jalia* lets herself get carried away as she begins to recount the road that brought her to Canada. She keeps her tuque on throughout our conversation, but wears a dark blue T-shirt that shows her arms. The burn scars draw attention, but her story gives way to vivid images, thanks to her rich powers of evocation, that carry us with her all the way to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Si elle a accepté de partager son histoi: If she agreed to share her story with La Converse, a story she normally keeps for her diary, it’s to make it clear that being an asylum seeker is not a choice, but a necessity. Especially when you leave everything behind, including a promising career.
“Cleaning isn’t easy. I get home and I have cramps; I even wake up at night because of those cramps. I didn’t have that before I started cleaning,” Jalia tells me toward the end of our interview. “There are weeks when I work seven days.”
La vie de la jeune femme de 27 ans n’a t: But the 27-year-old’s life wasn’t always like this.
Avocate de formation, elle réussit son b: A lawyer by training, she passed the bar in the DRC. “I was very involved in community organizations, for environmental causes, but also for women’s causes,” she explains. It was this activism that ended up costing her her safety in her country and that pushed her to apply for asylum in Canada last December, after the COP15 biodiversity conference held in Montréal.

Jalia tient à mentionner que son parcour: Jalia makes a point of mentioning that her university years were a real ordeal. First, she had to deal with several administrative problems – she wasn’t officially registered at the university, which nearly cost her her exams. Jalia also says she was bullied in the university residences. “If I left my clothes to dry on the clothesline, they would disappear and I’d see my classmates wearing them the next day, but I couldn’t say anything,” she says. That’s how Jalia learned that life isn’t simple and, above all, that it can be unfair.
Elle en a longtemps voulu à son père de: For a long time, she resented her father for putting her through this ordeal, during which she had to learn everything: washing her own clothes, cooking and… knowing hunger. Jalia believes this experience prepared her for her new life in Canada. “It was a very hard time, but I feel like my father wanted me to go through it so I would understand life,” says the woman, who grew up in a well-off Congolese family.
<strong>Quand l’engagement social oblige: When social engagement forces you to flee
Diplômée et avocate junior en RDC, Jalia: A graduate and junior lawyer in the DRC, Jalia could have settled for a position that would have allowed her to earn a very good living and enjoy the perks of her salary. Instead, she decided to get involved in a civil society group that promotes environmental protection as well as women’s rights.

« Souvent, nous allions sensibiliser les: “We often went to raise awareness about non-violence among young people and people in my province, particularly against child soldiers,” she recounts. “One day, we had an activity with young people, and after the activity, I went back to Goma, but the National Intelligence Agency summoned me.” That was the beginning of her ordeal.
Jalia sera détenue sans motif toute une: Jalia would be detained without cause for an entire night, after being locked for a few minutes in a cell full of men. “I went into the cell, and the men who were there tore off all my clothes; I screamed to the police officers for help. Afterward, I understood that it was a set-up, they just wanted to scare me. It was so I would stop what I was doing,” she whispers. These facts have not been verified by La Converse.
Son père finit par payer la caution pour: Her father eventually paid bail to get her out of detention, but ordered her to stay in a hotel.
« Ils sont venus la nuit dans mon hôtel: “They came to my hotel at night and they set it on fire. That’s when I got burned.
Je me suis réveillée dans une chambre en: I woke up in a room that was on fire and full of smoke,” Jalia recounts, showing her arms and neck. She still can’t explain how those people were able to get into her room.
Elle poursuit : « Des gens sont venus po: She continues: “People came to try to rescue me; they got me outside. They called the ambulance, which was supposed to take me to the hospital, but my father immediately drove me to the airport so I could leave for Kinshasa, the capital.”
Les cicatrices sont encore là, rappel co: The scars are still there, a constant reminder of the violence tied to her activism.
« Ensuite, j’ai reçu des menaces chaque: “After that, I got threats every day by phone” – an untenable situation.
Jusqu’à ce que son engagement pour l’env: Until her environmental commitment turned into a way out: she took part in COP15 in Quebec’s metropolis, a biodiversity summit she attended as an environmental activist from the DRC. It was once she was in Montréal that she filed an asylum claim.

Une fois sa demande d’asile déposée à Mo: Once her asylum claim was filed in Montréal, and as she had to leave the hotel where she had stayed during the COP15 conference, Jalia quickly realized that her options were limited. She obtained emergency temporary housing through the Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile (PRAIDA), an organization that helps asylum seekers when they arrive.
Débrouillarde, elle fait appel aux servi: Resourceful, she turned to the services of the Regroupement des organismes du Montréal ethnique pour le logement (ROMEL), which helps newcomers find housing, even if they don’t have many documents.
Jalia raconte : « Quand j’y suis arrivée: Jalia recounts: “When I got there, the person in charge told me I was lucky: a $700-a-month apartment was available. I took it on the spot, without seeing it!”
Et sans avoir l’argent ! Même si elle vo: And without having the money! Even though she no longer wanted to rely on her father, Jalia asked him for some money to pay the first two months’ rent. It would be the last time, and she takes a certain pride in that. Her life here, she is building it herself.
« Le responsable [chez ROMEL] m’a donné: “The person in charge [at ROMEL] gave me the key and the address of the place; I signed without even knowing where I was going.” It makes her laugh in hindsight, but it also reminds her of the urgency of finding a roof over her head at all costs.
« Quand je me suis rendue dans mon petit: “When I got to my little apartment, I didn’t have a bed, but it was already late. I put my clothes on the floor and I fell asleep. The next day, I went to get myself a bed, as a matter of urgency, and then someone told me about Marketplace, online.” A gold mine for finding all sorts of cheap items for her new life.
De fil en aiguille, Jalia trouve un empl: One thing leading to another, Jalia found a job… in Tadoussac. It was a job at a campground in that town on the Côte-Nord, more than six hours’ drive from Montréal.
« C’était une belle aventure, j’ai beauc: “It was a great adventure, I really loved it,” she says with a big smile. For two and a half months over the summer, it was the simple life, far from the hustle and bustle of the city. But she had to go back to Montréal, since it was a summer job. Another reality awaited her, one she dreaded: the fruitless job hunt.
Car durant tout son séjour à Tadoussac,: Because during her whole stay in Tadoussac, she didn’t sit idle: “I applied every day on LinkedIn, on Indeed; I even had interviews. Sometimes I did three interviews a day,” Jalia recounts. To no avail. “Either it was my English that let me down, because I didn’t know [the language] well enough, or I didn’t have enough experience in the field [I was applying in], which meant they didn’t take me.”
« C’est vraiment difficile de se rendre: “It’s really hard to realize how much Quebec experience counts, when you actually come with experience,” Jalia says indignantly.
Elle commence alors à gruger dans ses éc: She then started eating into her savings.
« Je m’étais dit que, plus jamais, je n’: “I had told myself that I would never again ask my father or anyone else for help.
Je suis restée à la maison un mois sans: I stayed home for a month with no income. Two months.” Time dragged on slowly, but money went faster. During our conversation, she relives that anxiety.
« Je me suis dit : “Je peux commencer à: “I told myself: ‘I can start cleaning people’s homes.’ On the one hand, I wondered: ‘Would I be able to do it?’ but on the other, I thought: ‘Will it pay my bills?’” she says, laughing, but with a laugh that hints at resignation.
C’est ainsi qu’elle prépare une annonce: So she put together an ad for Marketplace, where a few months earlier she had been buying everything she needed to furnish her apartment.
Mais au-delà de la nécessité de payer se: But beyond the need to pay her bills and eat, Jalia took up cleaning because she had another goal in mind: she wants to go back to school. “That’s what motivated me most to [do cleaning].”
« Ma première cliente se trouvait à Sain: “My first client was in Saint-Hyacinthe. I didn’t know where it was, but I accepted because I needed money,” she says, before describing her despair when she realized how far she had to travel.
« Ce n’était pas facile, avec le trajet: “It wasn’t easy, with the commute and all the work,” she says. “I came home half dead, half alive.” “The very next day, I wanted to delete the ad, but I had a lot of requests,” recounts the woman, who is woken at night by pain caused by the scrubbing.
« Ma vie ici au Québec et ma vie au pays: “My life here in Quebec and my life back home, it’s like the summit and the valley.”
Je lui demande si la vallée, ou le creux: I ask her if the valley, or the low point, is here. “Yes, it’s here, because I was a lawyer over there, I earned a lot of money, and my father also has a lot of money. So I was swimming in abundance,” she replies. Outings with friends at expensive restaurants, shopping, new phones were commonplace. But money doesn’t buy peace of mind.
Lorsqu’elle recevait des menaces et deva: When she was receiving threats and had to give workshops on climate change in villages, she had to pay a bodyguard to accompany her. An untenable situation. “That peace of being able to sleep, knowing that nobody is hunting me down, that I can come home whenever I want, I swear, it’s worth it,” she says.
Malgré tout, son temps est consacré aux: Despite everything, her time is devoted to others. Volunteering for several activities here in Montréal, including at a food bank, Jalia is still involved in her former activist association.
« Même en étant ici, je poursuis mon act: “Even being here, I continue my activism, campaigning against climate change and for the place of women in society, but by doing tasks that can be done online,” she says, as though it goes without saying, her conviction being stronger than anything.
« J’aime bien aider les autres, malgré m: “I really like helping others, despite my situation. Even when I’m cleaning, when people want to throw things away, I take them and we donate them at my church. When there are newcomers who need things, they can benefit from them.”
